Situation1: There is a scheduled family gathering on the calendar.
Situation2: Many prospects ask detailed technical questions about the new service that the script only partially addresses.
Story:
I stared at the calendar on my phone, the bright reminder for our family gathering blinking at me. My daughter had called last week, her voice warm, asking if I could come early to help set up. The grandkids were excited, she said, and I promised I’d bring my famous cookies. I wanted nothing more than to see their faces light up, to listen to their stories, to be the grandparent they remembered from summers past.

But my headset buzzed, snapping me back to the present. As a telemarketer, I was expected to stay on script, handle objections, and answer every technical question about our new service. Lately, the calls had been relentless—prospects grilling me on details the script barely covered. My supervisor’s emails were clear: “Don’t lose a single lead. We need your numbers up.” I felt the pressure mounting, the expectation to be available, to be knowledgeable, to never let a call go unanswered.

My heart tugged in two directions. I could almost hear my grandkids laughing in the backyard, but the reality of my job’s demands pressed in. I sat at my desk, torn, the clock ticking closer to the family gathering, my phone lighting up with another incoming call.
